title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
description: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to sto
body: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019, while it was still in development.In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.In 2025, Tesla sold just 20,237 Cybertrucks, a decline from 38,965 a year earlier, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book. Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 after commercial production of Cybertruck began in 2023.Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something "straight out of Blade Runner, external".But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it "ugly as sin, external".Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.  And then there's the price."We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

schema.headline: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
description: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon a
body: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries". The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood. Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock."The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties". Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".

schema.headline: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say

title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
description: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock val
body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall. The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI."The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today."I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure."The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said. "We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained."Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

schema.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values

title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenya doomsday cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for Shakahola deaths
description: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them child
body: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity."The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added. The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration."Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987. Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest". Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court. Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death. One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities. "We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023. Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings."It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence. Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

schema.headline: Paul Mackenzie: Kenya doomsday cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for Shakahola deaths

title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
description: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash k
body: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

schema.headline: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster

title: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension
description: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff betw
body: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule. But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives which has been used since 2012.Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary. But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach. The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency."Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

schema.headline: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension

title: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
description: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed
body: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approvalFigure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed archByNardine Saad and Isabella JewellReporting fromMemorial CircleA federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.  Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch. Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people. The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment."The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.It is not yet clear  when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project. The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court.""We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington CemeteryA rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office. The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones."There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments". How Trump is remaking the White House in his own imageHe and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended. Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".Image caption, Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the archOpponents have strongly disagreed. Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction."We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks. Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves". "This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch. It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m). His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch

title: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason
description: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raise
body: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement."By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement."The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court. He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty. Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice"."Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

schema.headline: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason

title: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in JanuaryByNardine SaadReporting fromLos Angele
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in JanuaryByNardine SaadReporting fromLos Angeles and Madeline HalpertCalifornia Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison. "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday. Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.Figure caption, Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in TennesseeDescribing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me"."As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote. "For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US. He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that"."I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centreNewsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence. Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions."At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said. Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action."These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said."By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty. "Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty. No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley. But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

schema.headline: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates

title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
description: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in
body: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely. No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday. As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them. Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public."Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week. Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities"."The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats."What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

schema.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines

title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallot
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes. Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentumSeveral prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger. Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressureExit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio."The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters."It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for futureBoth the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election."The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earnedBoth parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds. Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm."Neither party owns these voters," she said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina HinojosaThe Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend."Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said."After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

schema.headline: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race

title: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks
description: Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and c
body: Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.In the capital, Delhi, the air quality index (AQI) reached 391 on Friday morning, placing it in the "very poor" category ahead of the festival. There are fears that pollution levels could rise further after the celebrations.India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks, with its AQI reaching 322 on 24 October. Although air quality has improved in recent days to reach "moderate" levels of 104 on Friday, there are concerns that Diwali fireworks could trigger another spike.In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% less emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are in reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

schema.headline: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks

title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
description: Figure caption, Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answersByNick BeakeEurope correspondentRelatives of Britons killed in this summer
body: Figure caption, Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answersByNick BeakeEurope correspondentRelatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in."If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe."It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.'Issue the damned alert!'Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.Image source, Courtesy of the Chard familyImage caption, Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of BédarDuncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked."This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.The families reject that."Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true."The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze."The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future."They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."'A huge hole in our lives'Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church."They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave."They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.Image source, Danni Gillam-KirtonImage caption, Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their carThe fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human."We still don't know who or what they are," she said.Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents."It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.Image source, Gillam family handoutImage caption, Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Danni (second left) wants to know more about what happened to themThe letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario, a court order keeping the case file confidential.Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge."How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said."That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.Relatives say their fight is like David and Goliath."We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died."I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

schema.headline: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why

title: Indonesia's presidential wiretapping scandal: What to know
description: Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversat
body: Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign."Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian."So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping. Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution. In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes."It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian. "Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

schema.headline: Indonesia's presidential wiretapping scandal: What to know

title: Will Nigeria's Atiku Abubakar be on the presidential ballot after ADC court ruling?
description: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP
body: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - said he was shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC."The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected. "This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja

schema.headline: Will Nigeria's Atiku Abubakar be on the presidential ballot after ADC court ruling?
